Completeness: every nonempty set of them with an upper bound has a least upper bound, which the fractions lack (√2 leaves a gap); this makes them the only complete ordered field
Cantor’s 1874 paper showed the algebraic numbers can be listed but these cannot, so transcendental numbers must exist
Cantor proved (1877) that a square has no more points than a line segment, and wrote to Dedekind, “I see it, but I don’t believe it!”
Archimedean property: no matter which one of them you pick, some counting number is bigger
Computers store approximations of them in floating-point format (IEEE standard, 1985), so 0.1 + 0.2 often comes out as 0.30000000000000004
Even the interval from 0 to 1 holds uncountably many of them, as many as the whole line; they form a continuum with no gaps

trap.title: Real, rational, or complex?
trap.body: These numbers sit in the middle of a set of nested answer lines: the integers sit inside the rational numbers (fractions), which sit inside the real numbers, which sit inside the complex numbers. Irrational numbers like √2 and π are real but not rational. A tossup about √2 leaving a “gap” among the fractions may want rational numbers or real numbers, depending on what it asks for.
trap.fix: If the clues cover the whole number line, both fractions and irrational numbers, the symbol ℝ, Dedekind cuts, or Cantor’s proof that they can’t be listed, say “real numbers.” If every clue is about fractions p/q, say rational numbers; if the clues add i or a + bi, say complex numbers.
trap.line: Real answer line: real numbers (accept reals; prompt on R or number line; do not accept “rational numbers” or “complex numbers”)

topics.name: Bernhard Riemann
topics.kicker: Gauss’s student who reshaped geometry · His hypothesis is still unproven
topics.briefing: Bernhard Riemann was a shy German mathematician, a student of Carl Friedrich Gauss, who died of tuberculosis at just 39 but changed math forever. His 1854 lecture on the geometry of curved spaces later gave Albert Einstein the tools for general relativity, and Riemann sums estimate the area under a curve with rectangles. His 1859 guess about the zeros of the zeta function, the Riemann hypothesis, is still unproven, and proving it would win a $1 million prize.
topics.answerHtml: Bernhard Riemann (accept Riemann or Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Born in 1826 in the village of Breselenz in the Kingdom of Hanover, this son of a Lutheran pastor first enrolled at Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”] to study theology before switching to mathematics. He then studied in Berlin, where his teachers included Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician, a student of Carl Friedrich Gauss, whose hypothesis about the zeta function remains unproven.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss chose geometry, the last of three topics this man proposed, for his 1854 qualifying lecture, which described curved spaces of any number of dimensions. Albert Einstein later used this man’s geometry of curved spaces as the mathematical language of general relativity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose namesake sums estimate the area under a curve with rectangles.

tossups.p: When he was elected to the Berlin Academy in 1859, this man wrote “On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude,” his only paper on number theory. In it, he extended a function that Leonhard Euler had studied, now called the zeta function, to complex inputs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician whose namesake hypothesis says the nontrivial zeros of that function have real part one-half.

tossups.p: This man proved that the terms of 1 minus one-half plus one-third minus one-fourth, and so on, can be rearranged to add up to any number at all. In his 1854 qualifying thesis on trigonometric series, he defined the integral as a limit of sums.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose namesake sums use thin rectangles to estimate the area under a curve.

tossups.p: The function in this man’s most famous conjecture starts from the endless sum 1, plus 1 over 2 to the s, plus 1 over 3 to the s, and so on. When s equals 1, that sum becomes the harmonic series, which grows without limit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose hypothesis about the zeta function is a Millennium Prize Problem.

tossups.p: In 1914, G. H. Hardy proved that infinitely many of the zeros of a function named for this man lie on a “critical line,” where their real part is one-half. In 1900, David Hilbert grouped this man’s conjecture about those zeros with the Goldbach and twin prime conjectures in the eighth of his 23 famous problems.
tossups.r: A proof of that conjecture would win a $1 million Millennium Prize. For 10 points, name this German mathematician.

tossups.p: Marcel Grossmann helped his friend Albert Einstein learn this man’s geometry, including a curvature tensor named for this man, while Einstein was developing general relativity. A geometry with no parallel lines, in which a triangle’s angles add up to more than 180 degrees, is sometimes named for this man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician, a student of Gauss, whose hypothesis about prime numbers is still unproven.

tossups.p: This mathematician died of tuberculosis in 1866 in Selasca [“seh-LAHS-kah”], Italy, at age 39. His friend Richard Dedekind [“DAY-duh-kint”] later published this man’s famous 1854 lecture on geometry and helped edit his collected works.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose namesake sums approximate integrals and whose hypothesis concerns the zeta function.

tossups.p: This man shares a pair of equations with Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] that tell when a function of complex numbers has a derivative. His namesake sphere adds a single point at infinity to the plane of complex numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose hypothesis says the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function have real part one-half.

tossups.p: The “trivial” zeros of a function named for this man fall at negative 2, negative 4, negative 6, and so on. In 1896, Jacques Hadamard [“ah-dah-MAR”] and Charles de la Vallée Poussin [“vah-LAY poo-SAN”] used that function to prove the prime number theorem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician, whose namesake hypothesis about that zeta function remains unproven.

tossups.p: In 1859, this man succeeded Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”] as math professor at Göttingen [“GUHT-ing-un”]. David Hilbert reportedly said that if he woke up after sleeping for a thousand years, his first question would be whether this man’s hypothesis had been proven.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose namesake sums use thin rectangles to approximate the area under a curve.

tossups.p: This man’s 1851 doctoral thesis on functions of complex numbers introduced the surfaces now named for him. Leonhard Euler had found that the zeta function, which this man later extended to complex inputs, equals pi squared over 6 when its input is 2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician whose hypothesis about the zeros of the zeta function is unproven.

tossups.p: Henri Lebesgue [“luh-BEG”] later created a more general kind of integral than the one named for this man, which is the limit of sums of the areas of thinner and thinner rectangles. Those sums, named for him, can set each rectangle’s height at the left end, the right end, or the midpoint of its base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose namesake sums estimate the area under a curve.

tossups.p: This man’s 1859 paper gave an exact formula connecting the count of prime numbers to the zeros of a certain function, and computers have since checked trillions of those zeros without finding any off a single “critical line.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician whose hypothesis says all the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function lie on that line, where the real part is one-half.

tossups.p: A conjecture by this man appears both on David Hilbert’s 1900 list of problems and on the list of seven problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute announced in 2000. Leonhard Euler had linked the function in that conjecture to the primes by writing it as a product over all primes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German mathematician, a student of Gauss, whose hypothesis concerns the zeros of the zeta function.

trap.title: The man or his math?
trap.body: Many tossups want one of his namesakes instead of the man: the Riemann hypothesis, the Riemann zeta function, Riemann sums, or Riemannian geometry. If the question asks for “this conjecture,” “these sums,” or “this function,” naming the man is wrong. Early clues about complex numbers can also fit Augustin-Louis Cauchy (they share the Cauchy–Riemann equations) or his adviser, Carl Friedrich Gauss.
trap.fix: Life clues mean the man: a pastor’s son from Hanover, Gauss’s student at Göttingen, the 1854 lecture on geometry, or dying of tuberculosis in Italy at 39. If the giveaway asks for “this mathematician,” say “Riemann”; if it asks for “this hypothesis” or “these sums,” name the thing.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bernhard Riemann (accept Riemann or Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann)

topics.name: Derivatives
topics.kicker: The slope of a curve at a single point · The instantaneous rate of change
topics.briefing: A derivative tells you how fast something is changing at one exact instant, like the reading on a speedometer rather than your average speed for the whole trip. On a graph, it is the slope of the tangent line that just touches the curve at a point. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz each invented calculus in the late 1600s, and the derivative of position with respect to time is velocity.
topics.answerHtml: derivatives (or differentiation; prompt on slope or rate of change; do not accept “integral”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Gottfried Leibniz [“LYBE-nits”] first published his calculus in a 1684 paper whose title promised “a new method for maxima and minima, and also tangents.” The notation that writes this concept with a prime mark after the name of a function is named for Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNZH”].
tossups.r: Leibniz wrote it as d y over d x. For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a point.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton called this concept a “fluxion” and marked it with a dot above a letter; his _Method of Fluxions_ was written in 1671 but not published until 1736. Bishop George Berkeley’s book _The Analyst_ mocked the vanishing quantities used to define this concept as “ghosts of departed quantities.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the instantaneous rate of change of a function, which is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: The first calculus textbook, published in 1696 by the Marquis de l’Hôpital [“loh-pee-TAHL”], included a rule actually discovered by Johann Bernoulli [“ber-NOO-lee”] that finds a limit of the form 0 over 0 by taking this concept of the top and the bottom. Taking this concept of a function twice tells whether its graph curves up or down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written f prime of x, which gives the slope of a curve at a point.

tossups.p: Pierre de Fermat [“fair-MAH”] found the highest and lowest points of curves with a method he called “adequality,” decades before Newton and Leibniz developed calculus. A smooth function’s maximum or minimum inside an interval can occur only where this concept equals zero, so setting it equal to zero solves many optimization problems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function.

tossups.p: In 1872, Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] surprised mathematicians with a function that is continuous everywhere but has this quantity nowhere. The absolute value function has no value of this quantity at zero, because its graph has a sharp corner there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity from calculus, which equals the slope of the tangent line to a graph.

tossups.p: A theorem named for Michel Rolle, who proved a version of it for polynomials in 1691, says that if a smooth curve starts and ends at the same height, this quantity must equal zero somewhere in between. The mean value theorem generalizes that result: somewhere in between, this quantity equals the slope of the straight line joining the two endpoints.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written d y over d x, that gives a function’s instantaneous rate of change.

tossups.p: The fourth, fifth, and sixth versions of this concept for an object’s position are jokingly nicknamed snap, crackle, and pop, and the third is called jerk. This concept of velocity with respect to time gives acceleration.
tossups.r: Velocity is this concept of position with respect to time. For 10 points, name this calculus concept that measures an instantaneous rate of change.

tossups.p: Apart from its constant multiples, the function e to the x is the only function that equals its own value of this concept everywhere. This concept of the natural logarithm of x is 1 over x, and this concept of sine of x is cosine of x.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, developed independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz, that gives the slope of a curve.

tossups.p: The power rule says that this concept of x to the n equals n times x to the n minus 1, so for x cubed it is 3 x squared. This concept of any constant is zero, since the graph of a constant is a horizontal line with slope zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, which gives the instantaneous rate of change of a function and the slope of its tangent line.

tossups.p: The chain rule finds this concept for a function inside another function, while the product and quotient rules find it for products and quotients of two functions. This concept of a sum is the sum of this concept for each term.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, written f prime of x, which is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: Economists call this concept of total cost with respect to the number of items made the “marginal cost.” Related rates problems use this concept to find how fast the top of a ladder slides down a wall as its bottom is pulled away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of the tangent line, developed by both Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz.

tossups.p: Newton’s method finds a root of an equation by repeatedly subtracting the function’s value divided by this concept, which amounts to following tangent lines to where they cross the x-axis. A point where this concept changes from positive to negative marks a local maximum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept that gives the slope of a curve at a single point.

tossups.p: Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] helped make calculus rigorous by defining this concept as the limit, as h shrinks to zero, of f of x plus h, minus f of x, all over h. That fraction, before the limit is taken, is called a difference quotient.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, which gives the slope of the tangent line and is the reverse of integration.

tossups.p: At an inflection point, the second version of this concept changes sign, so the graph switches between curving up and curving down. If the second version of this concept is positive where the first version is zero, that point is a local minimum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the instantaneous rate of change, which gives velocity from position.

tossups.p: A 1712 report by the Royal Society, which Isaac Newton secretly helped write, credited Newton over Gottfried Leibniz for inventing the calculus of this concept. Partial versions of this concept, written with a curly d, are used for functions of several variables.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this calculus concept, the slope of a tangent line, which is the opposite of integration.

trap.title: Slope, not area
trap.body: Derivatives and integrals are opposite operations linked by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and both answer lines share clues about Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz. A derivative measures slope or an instantaneous rate of change, while an integral measures area or accumulation. Saying only “slope” or “rate of change” earns a prompt, and a tossup about one named rule (power, chain, product, L’Hôpital’s) may want that rule instead.
trap.fix: Listen for “slope,” “tangent line,” “rate of change,” “velocity from position,” “f prime,” or “d y over d x”: say “derivative.” “Area under a curve,” “antiderivative,” “accumulation,” or the long S symbol mean integral.
trap.line: Real answer line: derivatives (or differentiation; prompt on slope or rate of change; do not accept “integral”)

topics.name: Permutations
topics.kicker: Arrangements where order matters · There are n! ways to line up n objects
topics.dates: Bell-ringing orders described by Fabian Stedman, 1677
topics.briefing: A permutation is an arrangement of things in a particular order, so ABC and CBA are different permutations of the same three letters. There are n! ways to arrange n different objects, so three friends can line up in 6 ways, and a shuffled deck of 52 cards has a 68-digit number of possible orders. When order doesn’t matter, as when picking a team, you are counting combinations instead.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In December 1932, Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski [“reh-YEF-skee”] used the mathematics of these objects to work out the wiring of the rotors inside the German Enigma machine. Transposition ciphers scramble a message by applying one of these to its letters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects in which order matters, such as ABC and CBA.

tossups.p: In 1677, Fabian Stedman described change ringing, an English art in which a set of church bells is rung in one of these after another. Ringing all 5,040 of these on seven bells takes about three hours.
tossups.r: The number of these for n objects is n factorial. For 10 points, name these arrangements in which order matters.

tossups.p: Every one of these objects can be built from swaps called transpositions, and each one is classified as even or odd by the number of swaps it takes. That idea proves that the 15 puzzle can’t be solved once two of its tiles have been switched.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of a set of objects in which order matters, counted by n factorial.

tossups.p: The 8 corner pieces of a Rubik’s Cube can be placed in 40,320 of these, and counting them for its edge pieces helps show that the cube has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 reachable positions. Arthur Cayley proved that every group behaves like a group of these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects, which differ from combinations because their order matters.

tossups.p: In 1708, Pierre Rémond de Montmort [“mohn-MOR”] studied a card game asking how likely it is that no card lands in its matching place, a question now often told as the hat-check problem; the chance gets closer and closer to 1 over e. Those of these objects that leave nothing in its original place are called derangements.
tossups.r: There are n factorial of them for n objects. For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects in which order matters.

tossups.p: Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNZH”] and later Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”] studied how these objects shuffle the roots of a polynomial, explaining why some equations have no formula for their roots. Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] studied how these objects combine, work that helped launch group theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these orderings of a set of objects, which number n factorial for n objects.

tossups.p: Because its 11 letters include four S’s, four I’s, and two P’s, the word MISSISSIPPI has only 34,650 distinct ones of these, far fewer than 11 factorial. The word BOOK has only 12 of these, since swapping its two O’s changes nothing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rearrangements of letters or objects, counted with factorials, in which order matters.

tossups.p: A so-called “combination lock” would be better named after these, since entering its numbers in a different order will not open it. Gold, silver, and bronze medals can go to 3 of 8 runners in 8 times 7 times 6, or 336, of these.
tossups.r: Unlike combinations, these care about order. For 10 points, name these arrangements, n factorial in number for n objects.

tossups.p: A well-shuffled deck of 52 cards is almost certainly in an order no deck has ever had before, since 52 cards have a 68-digit number of these. Seating n people around a round table gives n minus 1 factorial of these, if rotations count as the same.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects in which order matters, which are different from combinations.

tossups.p: In cycle notation, one of these objects written (1 2 3) sends 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and 3 back to 1. On average, one of these chosen at random from all those of a set leaves exactly one object in its original place.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of a set of objects in which order matters, counted by factorials.

tossups.p: The Leibniz formula writes the determinant of a matrix as a sum over all of these objects, so a 4-by-4 determinant has 24 terms. Each of these objects is called even or odd, and the odd ones get a minus sign in that formula.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these orderings of a set of objects, which number n factorial for n objects.

tossups.p: B. R. Heap’s 1963 algorithm lists all of these objects for a set by switching just one pair of items at each step. Listed in dictionary order, these objects for the digits 1, 2, and 3 are 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, and 321.
tossups.r: There are n factorial of them for n objects. For 10 points, name these arrangements in which order matters.

tossups.p: Solving the traveling salesman problem by brute force means checking these objects of the cities, a number that grows faster than any exponential. Seven different books can be lined up on a shelf in 5,040 of these.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects in which order matters, unlike combinations.

tossups.p: The eighth-century Arab scholar al-Khalil ibn Ahmad is credited with using these objects to list all possible Arabic words, with and without vowels. Anagrams such as “listen” and “silent” are two of these objects made from the same letters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these arrangements of objects in which order matters, counted by n factorial.

tossups.p: All of these objects for a set of n things together form the symmetric group. Each combination of r objects matches r factorial of these objects, so there are r factorial times as many of these as there are combinations.
tossups.r: The number of them for n objects is n factorial. For 10 points, name these arrangements in which order matters.

The Leibniz formula for a determinant sums over all of these (odd ones get a minus sign), so a 4 × 4 determinant has 24 terms
B. R. Heap’s 1963 algorithm lists all of them by switching just one pair of items at each step
On average, a randomly chosen one leaves exactly one object in its original place (one fixed point)

trap.title: Order matters!
trap.body: Permutations and combinations both count ways to pick objects, and they are separate answer lines: in a permutation the order matters (gold, silver, bronze), while in a combination it doesn’t (picking a committee). Factorial is a third separate answer line: n! counts the permutations of n objects, but a tossup asking for “this function” written with an exclamation point wants factorial.
trap.fix: Listen for “order matters,” “arrangements,” “lined up,” or “rearranged”: say permutations. “Order doesn’t matter,” “choose,” “committee,” or Pascal’s triangle means combinations, and “this function, written with an exclamation point” means factorial. Saying only “arrangements” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: permutations (prompt on arrangements or orderings; do not accept “combinations”)
